   G-9 AND G-13 LANDOWNERS’ RESPONSE TO ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY
    COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION’S
    OBJECTIONS TO, AND MOTION TO STRIKE, INTERVENOR TESTIMONY

        The G-9 and G-13 Landowners1 file this Response to Oncor Electric Delivery Company

LLC (Oncor) and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation’s (LCRA TSC) (collectively,

Applicants) Objections to, and Motion to Strike, Intervenor Testimony.

                                        I.     INTRODUCTION

        On May 13, 2026, G-9 and G-13 Landowners filed the Direct Testimony of Jeffrey C.

Kubin on Behalf of The Highgate West Group, LLC and the Direct Testimony of James Giddens

on Behalf of the JKME Family Limited Partnership.2 Applicants filed their Objections to, and




         1
           The G-9 and G-13 Landowners include Jeff Kubin acting in the interest of The Highgate West Group LLC
(d/b/a The Highgate Group LLC) (owners of tract 2141), Bob Guthrie acting in the interest of Guthrie Ranching LTD
(owners of tracts 2127 and 2128), and James Giddens acting in the interest of JKME Family Limited Partnership
(owners of tracts 2147 and 5142).
        2
           Direct Testimony of Jeffrey C. Kubin on Behalf of The Highgate West Group, LLC (May 13, 2026) (Kubin
Direct); Direct Testimony of James Giddens on Behalf of the JKME Family Limited Partnership (May 13, 2026)
(Giddens Direct).


                                                       1
 Motion to Strike, Intervenor Testimony (Applicants’ Objection) on May 18, 2026.3 Service of the

Applicants’ Objection was provided to parties four days later on May 22, 2026. Although service

was not provided in a timely manner, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission or

PUC) Staff attorney confirmed with parties that the deadline to respond, pursuant to 16 Tex.

Admin. Code § 22.78, is within five working days – or May 26, 2026.

        Applicants’ objected to portions of the direct testimony of two G-9 and G-13 Landowners’

witnesses, James Giddens and Jeffrey C. Kubin. Specifically, Applicants object to the inclusion

of a letter from the Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF) which was filed on the PUC

interchange in this proceeding as an attachment to Mr. Giddens’ and Mr. Kubin’s testimony.

Applicants have the same objection for both James Giddens and Jeffrey C. Kubin. Therefore, this

Response addresses both objections at once.

                                  II.     RESPONSE TO OBJECTION

        G-9 and G-13 Landowners, through the Direct Testimony of Jeffrey C. Kubin on Behalf

of The Highgate West Group, LLC, and James Giddens on behalf of the JKME Family Limited

Partnership, voice their concerns regarding the G-9 and G-13 segments of the proposed

transmission line. In doing so, Mr. Giddens and Mr. Kubin each testify that they do not believe

the transmission line project has been properly vetted by the appropriate authorities.4 To better

support their position and arguments, they adopted and incorporated by reference the arguments

made in the TPPF’s letter to the Commission dated December 19, 2025 (Letter).5 Applicants

object to the use of the Letter on the grounds that it qualifies as expert opinion and hearsay pursuant



        3
          Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation's Objections to,
and Motion to Strike, Intervenor Testimony (May 18, 2026) (Applicants’ Objections).
        4
            Kubin Direct at 7; Giddens Direct at 8.
        5
            Id.


                                                      2
 to Texas Rules of Evidence 702, 801 and 802.6 Applicants’ Objection mischaracterizes the

purpose of the Letter in Mr. Giddens’ and Mr. Kubin’s testimonies. The intent of the Letter was

not to offer it to prove the truth of the matter asserted, nor provide expert opinion. Instead, Mr.

Giddens and Mr. Kubin adopt and incorporate the Letter to not only support their position that

they do not believe the project has been properly vetted and analyzed, but to incorporate those

arguments as both Mr. Giddens and Mr. Kubin note that the “issues should be addressed before

these transmission line routes are approved” and “before any construction begins.”7 Thus, the

Letter is included as a statement of position, not one of fact.

A. Inclusion of the Letter is not hearsay.

         Applicants argue that the TPPF Letter constitutes hearsay because it reflects statements of

individuals who are not parties to this proceeding and cannot be cross-examined.8 This objection

misapprehends both the nature of Mr. Giddens’ and Mr. Kubin’s use of the exhibit and the

applicable evidentiary framework in administrative proceedings.

         Under Texas Rules of Evidence 801, hearsay is defined as an out-of-court statement offered

to prove the truth of the matter asserted. Crucially, the out-of-court statement is not hearsay when

offered for a purpose other than establishing the truth of its contents—for example, to show that a

statement is made, or that concerns were publicly expressed.9




         6
             Applicants’ Objections, Exhibit A.
         7
             Kubin Direct at 7; Giddens Direct at 8.
         8
             Applicants’ Objections at 4.
         9
           Austin v. Hou. Lighting & Power Co., 844 S.W.2d 773, 791 (Tex. App.—Dallas 1992, writ denied) (“When
a party offers a statement simply to show that it was made rather than to show its truth or falsity, however, the hearsay
rule does not bar its admission. Further, newspaper articles not offered for the truth of the matters asserted but used
merely to show notice of those matters are not hearsay.”).


                                                           3
         In their direct testimony, Mr. Giddens and Mr. Kubin were asked “Do you believe that this

transmission line project has been properly vetted and analyzed by the appropriate authorities?”10

Each witness responded they strongly did not believe so, and both incorporated the Letter to

support the basis for that belief, as well as, incorporate the issues addressed in the letter into their

testimony as they should be addressed before the transmission routes are approved or construction

begins.11 Mr. Giddens and Mr. Kubin do not ask the Commission to accept as proven every factual

claim in the Letter. Rather, they offer the Letter to show that credible institutions and stakeholders

have raised similar concerns in a Letter questioning the project’s planning and necessity, and that

those concerns remained unresolved that the time of their testimony. Thus, the Letter is offered

not for the truth of the matter but instead was provided as a statement of position to show the

existence and public nature of those concerns, which is a proper non-hearsay purpose.12

B. Inclusion of the Letter is not expert opinion.

        Applicants further argue that the Letter should be stricken because it constitutes expert

opinion offered by an unqualified witness.13 This objection is both legally misplaced and factually

inaccurate as applied to Mr. Giddens’ and Mr. Kubin’s testimonies.

        Texas Rule of Evidence 702 governs the admissibility of expert testimony, requiring that

a witness be qualified by “knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education”14 before rendering

opinions on scientific, technical, or specialized matters. Applicants are correct that a lay witness’s

general familiarity with land or wildlife does not alone qualify that witness to render expert




        10
             Kubin Direct at 7; Giddens Direct at 8.
        11
             Id.
        12
             Hou. Lighting & Power Co., 844 S.W.2d at 791.
        13
             Applicants’ Objections at 2.
        14
             Tex. R. Evid. 702.


                                                       4
 opinions on transmission line engineering or medical science.15 However, that principle does not

apply to the facts in dispute.

       Mr. Giddens and Mr. Kubin are not offering expert testimony. They are testifying as

landowners about the nature, location, and use of their property, their observations of the proposed

routes’ proximity to habitable structures, concerns regarding the analysis of the project, and

personal concerns about the project’s impacts on their families, guests, and employees. Their

testimony falls squarely within the realm of lay opinion permitted by Texas Rule of Evidence 701,

which allows a non-expert to offer opinions that are rationally based on the witness’ own

perceptions and helpful to understanding the witness’ testimony or determining a fact in issue.

       As for the Letter itself, it is not being presented as expert opinion. In contrast, Mr. Giddens

and Mr. Kubin attached it to their testimony to further support the basis of their belief that the

project was not properly vetted.16 They do not adopt the letter’s technical content as their own

expert assertions—rather, they simply state the concerns addressed in the Letter are the same as

their own concerns and that those concerns should be addressed before the transmission line routes

are approved and construction begins. The Letter should not be struck from Mr. Giddens’ and Mr.

Kubin’s direct testimony as the Commission is capable of weighing the Letter’s policy analysis on

its own merits. Mr. Giddens and Mr. Kubin provide the Letter to further support the basis of their

belief that the project was not properly vetted which is not excluded under Rule 702.

                                          III.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons set forth above, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners respectfully request the

Administrative Law Judge deny Applicants’ Objection and Motion to Strike as applied to the
